title: Job 9:25–35
context: Job 9:25–35 completes Job’s reply in chapter 9 and is kept here as one unit. Job laments that his days are swifter than a runner, pass like swift ships, and swoop like an eagle (9:25–26; compare 7:6–7). The phrase rendered swift ships is understood by many as light boats made of reeds, and several modern translations render it that way, though the exact sense is uncertain. Job moves between speaking about God and speaking to him (9:28, 31), and says that no washing with snow or lye would make him clean in God’s sight (9:30–31). He ends with the complaint that God “is not a man, as I am” (9:32), and that “There is no umpire between us, that might lay his hand on us both” (9:33); older English versions use the word daysman, and some modern translations render the line as a wish for such an arbiter. He asks God to remove his rod and terror so that he could speak without fear (9:34–35; compare 13:21). Later in the book Job speaks of a witness in heaven (16:19–21) and of a Redeemer who lives (19:25), and Elihu speaks of an interpreter (33:23); how these passages relate to 9:33 is debated, and these notes name them without harmonizing. Christian readers in both traditions have commonly heard a later answer to Job’s longing in “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5); this is a common later reading, not the only sense of the verse, and it is shared ground rather than a point of contrast.

verses.text: “Now my days are swifter than a runner. They flee away. They see no good.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says, “Now my days are swifter than a runner. They flee away. They see no good.” Arminian readers note that the image recalls Job’s earlier lament that his days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle (7:6), and they hear the anguish of a life slipping past without relief or comfort.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo of 7:6–7 and the brevity of life as a theme across the wisdom books. They read the verse as Job’s honest lament, and they observe that his sense that his days see no good reflects his present suffering, not his whole life.

verses.text: They have passed away as the swift ships, as the eagle that swoops on the prey.
verses.arminianNotes: His days pass like swift ships and like an eagle swooping on its prey. Arminian readers note that the phrase rendered swift ships is understood by many as light reed boats, though the exact sense is uncertain, and they see the imagery of land, water, and air stressing speed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the identification of the boats loosely. They note that the three images of runner, ships, and eagle together build a picture of life rushing toward its end, a sober reminder both traditions draw from the wisdom literature.

verses.text: If I say, ‘I will forget my complaint, I will put off my sad face, and cheer up,’
verses.arminianNotes: Job imagines saying, ‘I will forget my complaint, I will put off my sad face, and cheer up,’ Arminian readers note that Job considers simply putting on a brave face, and they see in the verse a recognition that forced cheerfulness cannot remove real grief or answer real questions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job cannot simply decide to forget his complaint, because his suffering presses on him constantly. They read the verse as a realistic portrait of grief, and they caution against counseling sufferers to suppress lament for the sake of appearances.

verses.text: I am afraid of all my sorrows. I know that you will not hold me innocent.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says, “I know that you will not hold me innocent.” Here Job turns from speaking about God to addressing him directly. Arminian readers note that Job’s fear arises from his suffering, which he interprets as a sign that God has already judged him guilty, though the prologue shows otherwise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the shift to direct address, a feature that grows through Job’s speeches. They read Job’s fear as arising from his experience rather than from God’s actual verdict, and they observe that the LORD later speaks of “my servant Job” and his speaking rightly (42:7).

verses.text: I will be condemned. Why then do I labor in vain?
verses.arminianNotes: Job says, “I will be condemned. Why then do I labor in vain?” Arminian readers note that Job feels his efforts to prove his innocence are useless if he is already condemned, and they hear the weariness of a man who sees no point in further argument or striving.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job’s sense of futility reflects his assumption that God has already pronounced against him. They read the verse as lament, and they observe that both traditions see God’s eventual response to Job as showing that his labor in prayer and complaint was not in vain.

verses.text: If I wash myself with snow, and cleanse my hands with lye,
verses.arminianNotes: Job says, “If I wash myself with snow, and cleanse my hands with lye,” Arminian readers note that Job imagines the most thorough cleansing possible, and they see in the image his sense that no effort of his own could make him clean enough to satisfy God’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that washing with snow and lye pictures the greatest human efforts at purity. They see the verse as expressing a truth both traditions affirm, that self-cleansing cannot make anyone clean before God, though Job here speaks from despair rather than from a doctrine of grace.

verses.text: yet you will plunge me in the ditch. My own clothes will abhor me.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says God would plunge him in the ditch so that his own clothes would abhor him. Arminian readers note the vivid image of being made filthy again after washing, and they hear Job’s sense that God is determined to find him guilty, a perception the prologue shows to be mistaken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image of clothes abhorring the wearer heightens Job’s sense of defilement. They read the verse as Job’s anguished protest, and they observe that it is God, not Job, who will finally vindicate Job’s integrity before his friends (42:7–8).

verses.text: For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, that we should come together in judgment.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says, “For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him”. Arminian readers note that Job recognizes the vast difference between Creator and creature, which makes a fair trial seem impossible, and they treat God’s otherness as shared ground both traditions affirm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s transcendence is central to Reformed theology and is shared ground. They observe that Job feels this transcendence as a barrier to any meeting in judgment, a longing that the following verse expresses in its wish for someone to stand between them.

verses.text: There is no umpire between us, that might lay his hand on us both.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says, “There is no umpire between us, that might lay his hand on us both.” Arminian readers note that older English versions use the word daysman and some modern translations render the line as a wish, and they hold the readings open while hearing Job’s longing for an arbiter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Christians in both traditions have commonly heard a later answer in “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). They label this a common later reading, not the only sense of the verse, and they name 16:19–21 and 19:25 without harmonizing them.

verses.text: Let him take his rod away from me. Let his terror not make me afraid;
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks God to take his rod away and not let his terror make him afraid. Arminian readers note that Job asks for relief from the overwhelming sense of God’s power so that he can speak freely, and they compare his similar plea at 13:21, named here without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job’s request reveals how God’s majesty, felt in suffering, can silence a person. They read the verse as Job’s honest plea, and they observe that when the LORD does speak (38:1), Job is not destroyed but brought into a new understanding of God.

verses.text: then I would speak, and not fear him, for I am not so in myself.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says that then he would speak and not fear God, “for I am not so in myself.” Arminian readers note that the last phrase is of uncertain meaning, perhaps that Job does not see himself as guilty or that he is not as fearful as he appears, and they hold the sense open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the difficulty of the closing phrase and hold the readings open. They read the verse as Job’s desire for a fair hearing before God, a desire the book takes seriously and answers in its own way through the LORD’s speeches and the final verdict.
